title: A right in their wealth
hookLine: in their wealth was a right for the one who asks and the one deprived (51:19)

cards: Two people stand outside a grocery store. One holds a cardboard sign and asks everyone who passes.
The other, a few blocks away, has a job, an apartment, and an empty fridge she would never mention to anyone, not even her sister. The first is easy to see. The second you'd have to notice.
Surah Adh-Dhariyat names both of them, side by side, and says something about money that changes what giving even is.

teach.h: THE NIGHT PRAYER, THEN THE WEALTH.
teach.b: Verses fifteen to nineteen of Adh-Dhariyat describe the people of the gardens. They used to sleep little of the night. Before dawn, they asked forgiveness.
Then verse nineteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share." The Arabic is blunter. Wa fi amwalihim haqqun: and in their wealth, a right.

teach.h: HAQQ: TRUTH, AND WHAT IS OWED.
teach.b: Haqq means truth, and it also means what is owed, what someone is entitled to. So the poor don't receive a favor from these people. They receive what was already theirs, held for a while in someone else's account.
Then the two who are owed.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO ASKS, AND THE ONE WHO WON'T.
teach.b: As-sa'il: the one who asks. And al-mahrum: the deprived. Ibn Kathir and other commentators explain the mahrum as the one in need who doesn't ask, whose dignity keeps them silent, whom you'd have to notice to help.
The verse puts the silent one right next to the asking one. A similar verse in Surah Al-Ma'arij says a known right, haqqun ma'lum, which some commentators connect to zakat, the fixed annual alms.
Others read the verse here as reaching beyond it, to generosity on top of what was required. Notice the order: night prayer, then forgiveness before dawn, then wealth.
In this passage, worship doesn't stay in the prayer room; for these people, it ended in their accounts. In the verse's terms, giving isn't a kindness done.

how: Muslims pay zakat, a fixed share of savings, once a year to set categories of people in need, and give voluntary sadaqah beyond it, often quietly, to protect the dignity of those who don't ask.

o: a gift given freely from kindness alone
a tax paid to the ruler of the land
a right: what is truly owed to someone

games.q: a right in their wealth — tap the pairs.
p: the deprived one who doesn't ask

s: in 51:19, giving to the poor is described as a favor
the Arabic says haqq: a right, something owed.
the verse names a needy person who doesn't ask
al-mahrum, the deprived, often silent out of dignity.
in the surah, the verse about wealth comes right after night prayer and seeking forgiveness
worship that ends in their accounts.

games.q: you have something to give. by 51:19, who should you be looking for, besides the person who asks?
o: the deprived one who won't ask.
games.why: the verse puts al-mahrum, the silent one in need, right beside the one who asks.

practice: Think slowly through the people around you, family, coworkers, neighbors, the friend who's gone quiet, and ask who might be struggling without saying it.
Look for small signs, a canceled plan, a too-quick change of subject, and think of a way to give that protects their dignity, help offered without fuss. If you pray, you can ask to notice.

wordCard.voice: Haqq: in 51:19, the share owed to the one who asks and to the deprived one who doesn't. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a right, not a favor. The quiet ones are owed too. That's day five hundred ninety-four.
